performers: Hochschulsymphonieorchester, University of Music and Theatre Munich; Marcus Bosch, conductor
intro: The finale turns the symphony’s long opening melody into a nimble violin tune with sharply dotted rhythms. Three very different themes return in reverse order before the horns recover the first movement’s broad E-major melody.

cues.title: A new gait for old notes
cues.text: First violins give the symphony’s opening notes a quick, double-dotted rhythm. Second violins tremble underneath; cellos and basses take up the tune next. The first movement’s enormous melody has acquired short steps and a spring in its heels.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition (1885), IV, opening and letter A, p. 71. The relation between the two opening themes is described by the Berlin Philharmonic: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/symphony-no-7-in-e-major/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A chorale on plucked basses
cues.text: The violins settle into long, quiet notes in A♭ major. Violas add an answering line; cellos and basses pluck a bass that moves by semitones. The chorale seems still at first, but those moving lower voices keep changing the colour of its chords.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter C, pp. 72–73: the chorale in the violins, violas and plucked cellos and basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: No Wagner tubas at first
cues.text: A discarded first page of the finale has no staves for Wagner tubas. Bruckner apparently planned this movement without them, says Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs, who edited the score. The finished finale uses them.
cues.evidence: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs, booklet note for the Hyperion recording of the Seventh (2023), on the surviving discarded bifolio with no staves for Wagner tubas: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: The last page in September
cues.text: Bruckner finishes the finale’s sketch on 10 August 1883 and its orchestral score on 5 September. Nearly two years separate that last page from the first, dated 23 September 1881 at St Florian.
cues.evidence: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs, booklet note (2023), dates the opening page, finale sketch and completed score: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: One melody across the orchestra
cues.text: Strings, woodwinds and brass stride together through the third theme in A minor. Octave doublings give it a blunt, muscular sound. The strings are told to bow strongly throughout; schwer asks for weight on the falling phrase.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter F, p. 75: immer markig gestrichen and schwer; the horns’ first notes (written e″, b′, g′ for horn in F) sound a′, e′ and c′, an A-minor triad.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A toccata in the dotted rhythm
cues.text: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs hears an organ toccata in the obstinate dotted rhythm of the finale’s opening tune and of this third theme. The powerful third theme and its restatement, he says, form the centre of the movement.
cues.evidence: Cohrs, booklet note for the Hyperion recording of the Seventh (2023), on the finale’s dramaturgy and the organ-toccata rhythm of the first and third themes: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: The strings leave a wind conversation
cues.text: The strings stop. Flute, oboe and clarinet pass a quiet phrase down through the woodwind, then Wagner tubas answer. A few soft timpani notes on C remain from the preceding passage before the drum also falls silent.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letters L–M, p. 79; wind exchanges, tuba answers, string rests and timpani C.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keys a major third apart
cues.text: Bruckner sets the finale’s main ideas in E major, A♭ major and C major, keys a major third apart that divide the octave into three equal parts. The usual relations by fifths play only a minor part.
cues.evidence: Analysis of the Seventh from the University of Music and Theatre Munich (Open Music Academy): the finale’s key plan is dominated by major-third (mediant) relations that divide the tonal space into three equal parts. https://openmusic.academy/docs/bmwvSwGA9xQFLhfL4GJukj/anton-bruckner-sinfonie-nr7-e-dur-wab-107

cues.title: Wolf and Levi are baffled
cues.text: The composer Hugo Wolf and the conductor Hermann Levi both found parts of this finale incomprehensible. Both came round, in the end, to its unique beauty.
cues.evidence: Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note on the Seventh (both men found certain parts of the finale “incomprehensible” and eventually came to appreciate it): https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/

cues.title: A finale like Haydn’s
cues.text: The conductor Georg Tintner called this finale, next to the rest of the symphony, “more like the finale in a Haydn symphony”. It runs about thirteen minutes against the first movement’s twenty-two; the Fifth’s finale runs twenty-three minutes against nineteen, the Eighth’s twenty-one against fourteen.
cues.evidence: Tintner’s booklet note on the Seventh (Naxos 8.554269), as quoted by Ates Orga in BBC Music Magazine: https://www.classical-music.com/reviews/orchestral/bruckner-87 (the booklet itself not opened). Approximate timings of the finales and first movements of the Seventh, Fifth and Eighth: Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note, https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/

cues.title: The chorale comes back quietly
cues.text: The orchestra stops on a held note. Violins begin the chorale again over plucked cellos and basses; oboe, clarinet and horn join its long phrases. The third theme has returned before the second. Bruckner is bringing the themes home in reverse order.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter S, p. 85. Reversed order of recapitulation described by the Hungarian National Philharmonic: https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nikisch at the second piano
cues.text: Arthur Nikisch plays through the new symphony on two pianos with Bruckner’s pupil Josef Schalk. He decides to conduct it with the Gewandhaus Orchestra. On 30 December 1884, that private encounter becomes the Seventh’s Leipzig premiere.
cues.evidence: Two-piano reading and Nikisch’s decision: Hungarian National Philharmonic, https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/. Premiere date and performers: Berlin Philharmonic programme note.

cues.title: “The most important since 1827”
cues.text: Bruckner reports to a friend in Linz that Hermann Levi has called the Seventh “the most important symphonic work since 1827”, the year Beethoven died. Levi later calls it a Wunderwerk and the “crowning event” of his career as a conductor.
cues.evidence: Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note: Bruckner’s report to a friend in Linz of Levi’s remark, and Levi’s “Wunderwerk” and “crowning event”: https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/

cues.title: Horns above a rolling E
cues.text: A quiet timpani roll on E begins beneath repeated string chords. Horns enter in pairs with the dotted tune; trumpets follow, then the woodwinds sustain the harmony above them. Each new voice adds to the crescendo without disturbing the bass note.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter Z, pp. 96–97: Tempo I, anfangs noch sehr ruhig, timpani E and successive brass entries.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first melody stands revealed
cues.text: The horns stretch the dotted tune back into the symphony’s broad opening melody. Trumpets and clarinets answer with its descending shape while the violins continue their quick figures. E major holds beneath them all, with the timpani rolling to the last chord.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, final nine bars, pp. 98–99. The return of the first movement’s original theme in these bars is identified by the Berlin Philharmonic programme note.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The dotted tune gives way to long notes
transitions.from: A · A dotted tune above trembling strings
transitions.to: B · Strings sing an A♭-major chorale
transitions.how: Horn chords and the last violin figures diminish. At rehearsal C, the pace broadens and violins begin the A♭-major chorale in long notes. Violas answer beneath them while cellos and basses pluck a chromatically moving bass. Wagner tubas enter as the phrase continues.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition (1885), IV, letter C, pp. 72–73.

transitions.title: The strings summon the orchestra in octaves
transitions.from: B · Strings sing an A♭-major chorale
transitions.to: C · The orchestra strides in A minor
transitions.how: The quiet string phrases gain weight through a crescendo. At F, winds, brass and strings begin the third theme together in A minor, doubled across several octaves. Repeated accents and the marking schwer give its falling notes a heavy tread.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter F and preceding bars, p. 75.

transitions.title: Timpani linger as the strings stop
transitions.from: C · The orchestra strides in A minor
transitions.to: Link · Winds and tubas without strings
transitions.how: The string figures diminish and stop, leaving a few soft timpani notes on C. Flute begins a phrase which passes to oboe and clarinet; the Wagner tubas answer. The drum drops out too, leaving the winds and brass to continue alone through Ruhig and the following a tempo.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letters L–M and preceding bars, p. 79.

transitions.title: The dotted figures gather brass and strings
transitions.from: Link · Winds and tubas without strings
transitions.to: D · Dotted figures gather the full orchestra
transitions.how: The short dotted figures gather strength through the orchestra. Winds and brass carry emphatic, separately marked notes against the running strings. The passage expands towards Q, Breit und wuchtig — broad and weighty — followed by immer breiter, broader still.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letters P–R, pp. 81–84; marcato figures and broadening instructions.

transitions.title: A held note opens onto quiet strings
transitions.from: D · Dotted figures gather the full orchestra
transitions.to: B′ · The quiet string chorale returns
transitions.how: The whole orchestra converges on a held note with a pause. At S, Tempo I, strings begin the chorale softly over plucked cellos and basses. Oboe enters first, followed by clarinet and horn; trumpets and low brass remain silent.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter S and preceding bars, p. 85.

transitions.title: Flute and violins rise above the brass
transitions.from: B′ · The quiet string chorale returns
transitions.to: E · Broad brass beneath climbing violins
transitions.how: A crescendo in winds and strings reaches V, marked Breit. Flutes and first violins climb in fast figures. Horns, trumpets, trombones and tubas answer with the dotted rhythm, while second violins and violas give the chords a firm repeated pulse.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter V, p. 88.

transitions.title: The strings restart the dotted figure softly
transitions.from: E · Broad brass beneath climbing violins
transitions.to: Link · Quiet strings rebuild the dotted tune
transitions.how: The orchestral chords slow and diminish. X restores a tempo: first violins, violas and low strings exchange quiet dotted figures above second-violin tremolo. Oboe supplies a longer phrase, then horn and trumpet join the gradual crescendo towards Y.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letters X–Y and preceding bars, pp. 93–94.

transitions.title: The broad chords yield to a drum roll
transitions.from: Link · Quiet strings rebuild the dotted tune
transitions.to: Coda · Horns rise above the timpani roll
transitions.how: The full orchestra broadens into accented chords. At Z the brass withdraw, leaving quiet repeated string chords and a timpani roll on E. Tempo I begins very calmly. Horns enter in pairs, then trumpets, as the crescendo gathers above the unchanging bass.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter Z, p. 96: Tempo I, anfangs noch sehr ruhig.

source.title: Bruckner, Symphony No. 7, full score (Vienna: A. J. Gutmann, 1885, plate A.J.G. 576; first edition)
source.locator: IV. Finale, printed pp. 71–99; opening and letters A, C, F, L–M, P–S, V and Z. The horn group includes the Wagner tubas.

timeline.note: First violins begin the dotted melody above second-violin tremolo; violas join beneath them.
Cellos and basses take up the dotted tune; woodwind phrases answer above them.
The chorale in A♭ major: the strings carry the melody; Wagner tubas and horns later colour it.
The octave theme in A minor for the whole orchestra, heavily accented.
Flute, oboe and clarinet exchange phrases, followed by Wagner tubas; a few timpani notes remain as the strings stop.
The heavy tutti returns, winds and brass marked “marc. sempre”.
The quiet chorale returns at “Tempo I”, with winds and strings.
The broad tutti at letter V, “Breit”, for the whole orchestra.
A quiet timpani roll on E supports repeated string chords and successive horn entries.
A crescendo for the whole orchestra over the timpani tremolo, to the final E major chord.

composer.epithet: He spent half his life learning his trade, then wrote symphonies in which a horn call can grow into a wall of brass.
facts: St Florian; counterpoint with Simon Sechter, 1855–61; composition with Otto Kitzler, 1861–63
Organist at St Florian and Linz; Vienna Conservatory from 1868; university lecturer from 1875
Nine numbered symphonies, two outside the sequence; masses, motets and secular choral music
The Seventh Symphony, Leipzig, 30 December 1884; Arthur Nikisch conducting
composer.background:
On 16 December 1877 Bruckner stood before the Vienna Philharmonic to conduct his Third Symphony. Johann Herbeck, who had intended to conduct it, had died in October. The audience began to leave. Among the supporters who stayed was the seventeen-year-old Mahler, who helped turn the enormous score into a piano duet. Bruckner was fifty-three, a conservatory professor and an internationally admired organist. In the concert hall he was still having to introduce himself.

He was born in Ansfelden, near Linz, where his father taught school and played church music. After his father died in 1837, his mother took him to the Augustinian abbey of St Florian as a choirboy. He learned the organ, trained as a teacher and worked in the villages of Windhaag and Kronstorf. In Windhaag he also played the fiddle for dancing. The heavy-footed country dances in his scherzos had passed through his hands long before he wrote for an orchestra.
